question: What three kinds of animal may be offered as a burnt offering, and what gestures are repeated in each case?
The word עֹלָה (olah, “burnt offering”) comes from the verb “go up”: what does this offering, burned whole and “going up” to the LORD, express about the self-giving of the one who brings it?
What might it mean for the worshiper to lay his hand on the animal's head before it is offered?
The law accepts anything from a bull to two birds: what does this say to you about the worth of the offering of someone who has little?
What ingredients are required in the grain offering, and which are forbidden?
The word אַזְכָּרָה (azkarah, “memorial portion”) names the portion burned on the altar: what does it mean for an offering to serve as a “memorial” before the LORD?
What might the expression “the salt of the covenant of your God” mean, and why must it not be missing from any offering?
The grain offering came from daily work in the field and the kitchen: how could you offer God the fruit of your ordinary work?
What parts of the animal are burned in the peace offering, and what does verse 16 say about the fat?
The word שֶׁלֶם (shelem, “peace offering”) is related to שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace”): what relationship between the worshiper, God and the community might this offering celebrate?
Why is the ban on eating fat and blood given as a “permanent statute” in all your dwellings?
The peace offering was not to make up for a wrong but to celebrate fellowship: at what moments do you thank God without asking for anything?
Who can sin according to this chapter, and what changes in the rite according to each person's position?
The word שְׁגָגָה (shegagah, “unintentionally, in error”) is repeated: what does it mean to be responsible even for sin committed without intent?
Why do the sin of the anointed priest and that of the whole congregation require a weightier rite than that of an ordinary person?
The text speaks of a sin that was “hidden from the eyes of the assembly” until it was understood: what collective mistake of your community have you only recently begun to notice?
What situations make someone guilty, according to verses 1 to 4?
The verb יָדָה (yadah, “confess”) appears in verse 5, before the offering: what role does confession play on the way to forgiveness?
What does the sequence of simpler offerings (birds, flour) for those without means show?
Whoever sinned in regard to the holy things must make restitution and add a fifth: what concrete amends do you still owe someone?
What kinds of fraud against a neighbor does the text list, and what must the guilty person do before bringing the offering?
The verb כָּבָה (kavah, “go out, be quenched”) appears in the command that the fire on the altar “must not go out”: what might this ever-burning flame have reminded the people and the priests of?
Why is an offense against one's neighbor also called “unfaithfulness against the LORD”?
Restitution comes before the rite: what debt with someone do you need to settle before seeking peace with God?
What rules apply to the peace offering of thanksgiving, and how soon must its meat be eaten?
The word תּוֹדָה (todah, “thanksgiving”) names a kind of peace offering: what does it mean for gratitude to have its own rite, shared in a meal?
Why are certain parts of the sacrifices given to the priests as a “permanent portion”?
The meat of the thank offering had to be eaten the same day: how could you thank God without putting off your gratitude?
In what order does Moses wash, clothe and anoint Aaron and his sons before the congregation?
The word מִלֻּא (millu, “ordination,” linked to the idea of “filling the hands”) names the ram of verse 22: what does it mean to have one's hands “filled” for a service?
Why must the priests stay seven days at the entrance of the tabernacle before beginning their service?
“They did everything the LORD had commanded”: what step of preparation have you been skipping in some task that requires care?
What happens on the eighth day, and for whom must Aaron offer first?
The promise that “the glory of the LORD will appear to you” (v. 6) is fulfilled in verse 23: what does it mean for the כָּבוֹד (kavod, “glory”) to appear “to all the people”?
How do the people react when fire comes out from the presence of the LORD, and why do they shout for joy instead of fleeing?
Aaron and Moses bless the people as they come out of the tabernacle: whom do you bless after your times with God?
What do Nadab and Abihu offer, and what is the consequence?
The “unauthorized fire” uses the verb זוּר (zur, “be strange, foreign”): what might have made that fire unauthorized, according to verse 1 itself?
What task do the priests receive in verses 10 and 11, and why does it require sobriety?
“And Aaron remained silent”: in the face of a pain or loss you do not understand, what room do you give to silence?
What criteria does the text use to sort the land animals, the water creatures and the insects that may be eaten?
The word קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh, “holy”) appears at the end of the chapter: how does the phrase “be holy, because I am holy” give meaning to all the rules about food?
According to verses 46 and 47, what is this law for, and how has it been read in Judaism and in Christianity?
Holiness here passes through what is eaten every day: in what ordinary choices of your routine do you express, or could you express, your faith?
What periods of uncleanness and purification are set after the birth of a boy and of a girl?
The word טׇהֳרָה (tohorah, “purification”) describes the mother's time after giving birth: what might this period away from holy things have meant for her?
Why does the law provide a simpler offering for those who cannot afford a lamb?
The text adjusts the offering to the family's means: how can you make the life of your community accessible to those who have little?
What signs on the skin must the priest examine, and what does he do when the case is not yet clear?
The word צָרַעַת (tsaraat), translated “leprosy,” covered various skin diseases and even marks on clothing: what changes in the reading when you realize it is not just today's Hansen's disease?
What did it mean for someone to have to cry “Unclean!” and live outside the camp?
Who lives “outside the camp” today because of illness or stigma, and how could you draw near to these people?
What does the priest do with the two birds in the cleansing ritual, and what happens to the live bird?
The verb טָהֵר (taher, “be clean, cleanse”) runs through the chapter: what stages does the person go through until being declared clean and returning to the life of the community?
What link is there between the blood and oil placed on the ear, thumb and toe of the cleansed person and the consecration of the priests in 8:23-24?
The priest “is to go outside the camp” to see the sick person: what does it mean to go to those who are excluded, instead of waiting for them to come?
How is the uncleanness of a discharge passed on, according to verses 4 to 12, and what must the person do to be cleansed?
The verb זוּב (zuv, “flow, have a discharge”) gives the theme of the whole chapter: why did bodily matters, which are not sin, have rules linked to worship?
What reason does verse 31 give for all these laws, and what does it reveal about God's presence “among them”?
This chapter deals with intimate matters frankly: how can faith help you deal with your own body without shame and with care?
What animals does Aaron take from the congregation, and how is the fate of each of the two goats decided?
The name עֲזָאזֵל (azazel) has a debated meaning (a place, a desert being, or “the goat that goes away”): what image does the goat sent into the wilderness, carrying the iniquities, offer the reader?
Why is it necessary to cleanse not only the people but also the sanctuary and the altar, according to verses 16 to 19?
The Day of Atonement asks the people to “humble yourselves” and rest: what place do self-examination and repentance have in your calendar?
Where must every animal be sacrificed, according to verses 3 to 9, and what old practice does the text want to prevent?
The word נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, “life, soul”) appears in verse 11 with the blood: what does it mean to say that “the life of the flesh is in the blood”?
How does the ban on eating blood relate to respect for life, even in hunting animals?
The text treats the life even of an animal with reverence: how can this influence the way you see the life around you?
What practices must the people avoid, and from what lands did they come, according to verses 3 to 5?
The verb חָיַי (chayay, “live”) appears in verse 5: what does it mean to say that whoever keeps God's statutes “will live by them”?
How did these laws protect family ties and the most vulnerable, and how do Jews and Christians of different traditions read them today?
The land that “vomits out” its inhabitants is a strong image: what practices of our society do you think make common life sick?
What commandments about harvest, work and the court appear in verses 9 to 18, and whom do they protect?
The verb אָהַב (ahav, “love”) appears in verse 18 for the neighbor and in 34 for the foreigner: what changes when the same love is asked for both?
How does the phrase “Be holy because I am holy” translate in this chapter into concrete everyday attitudes?
Leaving the corner of the field for the poor and the foreigner was a law: what “corner” of your income or your time could you leave for those in need?
What religious practices does the chapter condemn right at the start, and what is expected of the people of the land in response?
The verb בָּדַל (badal, “set apart”) appears three times at the end: what does it mean that God “set apart” Israel from the peoples to be “Mine”?
How should laws with such severe penalties be read today, and how have the Jewish and Christian traditions dealt with their application?
“I am the LORD who sanctifies you”: what changes when holiness is seen as God's work and not only as human effort?
What restrictions apply to the priests regarding mourning and marriage, and what more is required of the high priest?
The word מאוּם (mum, “defect”) excludes some of Aaron's descendants from offering at the altar: what does verse 22 still guarantee them?
Why does the service of the altar require so much care for the holiness of those who perform it?
Those with a defect still ate “the food of his God”: how does your community welcome people with disabilities and make sure they are part of it?
Who may and who may not eat the sacred offerings in the priest's household, according to verses 10 to 13?
The verb רָצָה (ratsah, “accept, be pleased with”) is linked to the requirement of animals without defect: what does it mean for an offering to be “accepted” by God?
What care for animals appears in verses 27 and 28, and what might it teach beyond the rite?
Offering God a defective animal was offering what was left over: in what have you been giving God only the leftovers of your time or energy?
What are the appointed feasts of the LORD through the year, and on what month and day does each one take place?
The word סֻכָּה (sukkah, “booth”) gives its name to the feast of the seventh month: what were the people to remember by living seven days in booths?
Why does the law of the harvest for the poor and the foreigner appear in the middle of the list of feasts?
“Rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days”: what place do joy and celebration have in your life of faith?
What happens between the son of the Israelite woman and another man, and how does the case come to a decision?
The verb נָקַב (naqav, “pronounce, blaspheme”) is used for the one who “blasphemed the Name” in cursing: why is God's name treated so seriously in this law?
How do you understand the rule that there be “the same law” for the foreigner and the native, even in penalties?
The lamps were to burn continually with oil brought by the people: what do you contribute to keep your community's faith alive?
How is the Year of Jubilee counted, when is it proclaimed, and what happens to lands and families in that year?
The word יוֹבֵל (yovel, “jubilee,” linked to the sound of the trumpet) marks the year when “liberty is proclaimed in the land”: what kind of fresh start did this law guarantee each generation?
What reason does God give in verse 23 for the land not being sold permanently, and what does this say about property?
“If your brother becomes impoverished… you are to help him”: what concrete form could this help take in your life today?
What blessings are promised to those who walk in God's statutes, and what is their high point in verses 11 and 12?
The word קְרִי (qeri, “hostility, opposition”) is repeated in the expression “walk in hostility toward Me”: what relationship does the text describe between the people's attitude and God's response?
Even after so many threats, what does the end of the chapter promise those who confess their iniquity?
God says He made the people “walk with heads held high”: from what yoke do you need to be freed to live this way?
How are people dedicated by vow valued, and what happens when the one who made the vow is poor?
The word מַעֲשֵׂר (maaser, “tithe”) appears in the last verses of the book: what does it mean for the tenth of the land and the herd to be called “holy to the LORD”?
Why can an animal that has been vowed not be exchanged, “good for bad or bad for good”?
The chapter deals with vows made to God: what promise have you made to God or to someone, and how have you taken care to keep it?
